docs.title: Qasmith Documentation
docs.text: Welcome to the Qasmith documentation. Qasmith is a high-level quantum programming language for developers who want familiar functions, modules, and packages.

docs.title: What is Qasmith?
docs.text:
Qasmith compiles reusable .smith modules to OpenQASM 3.0 and includes a local ideal statevector simulator. The language provides:

  • Familiar syntax - TypeScript-like syntax with functions, modules, and packages
  • Type safety - Strong typing with Int, Float, Qubit, and MeasuredResult
  • Resource management - Owned qubits with borrow checking
  • Quantum gates - Standard gates: x, h, cx, rx, ry, rz
  • Optimization - Built-in QUBO, Ising, and QAOA support
  • Simulation - Local statevector simulator with shot-based execution

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Install Qasmith and create your first quantum program:

# Install (macOS/Linux)
curl -fLO https://github.com/quvly/Qasmith/releases/latest/download/install.sh
sh install.sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

# Verify installation
qasmith version

Create a Bell state circuit:

fn main() -> MeasuredResult {
    let a = qubit();
    let b = qubit();
    h(a);
    cx(a, b);
    return measure(a, b);
}

Compile and run:

qasmith compile bell.smith
qasmith run bell.smith --shots 1000

docs.title: Compiler architecture
docs.text:
The source loader finds the entry manifest and resolves imports as parsing discovers them. The resulting graph has one AST per canonical source module. Semantic analysis declares signatures, binds imports to exported symbols, validates every function body, and associates call expressions with their targets. A call-graph traversal finds recursion and propagates distinct-qubit constraints up the graph.

Lowering evaluates static scalars and immutable arrays. It binds arguments in per-call frames, evaluates indexing and conditions, and expands each loop in order. Register allocation reserves consecutive logical IDs. Helper parameters carry the caller’s register base and size. Lowering inlines quantum calls using those same IDs. Arithmetic failures point to the operator and report active source call sites. check type-checks the full dependency graph and evaluates reachable compile-time constructs with host callbacks disabled. Values that require a callback, and checks that depend on them, are resolved when compiling or evaluating. The IR can be validated, passed through optional optimizations, emitted by a backend, or simulated directly.

docs.title: Circuit IR
docs.text:
The public pkg/ir package represents a circuit as an ordered list of these value operations:

Operation Operands Semantics AllocateQubit QubitID Create a logical qubit initialized to zero. IDs begin at zero and increase in allocation order. ApplyGate Gate, ordered qubit IDs, optional numeric parameters Apply X or H to one live qubit, CX to a distinct control and target in that order, or RX, RY, or RZ with one finite Float64 angle in radians. Measure QubitID, BitID Measure a live qubit in the computational basis. Consecutive result IDs start at zero.

Measurements form a terminal block. A qubit may be measured once. Program.Validate checks the sequence and returns register sizes. Optional origin metadata identifies the operation's source and active call sites from innermost to outermost.

Source registers, loops, arrays, and branches are resolved before IR validation. Backends and passes continue to work with the same flat logical qubit IDs and operations.

docs.title: OpenQASM 3 and simulation
docs.text:
The default backend declares qubit[N] q and bit[M] c, includes stdgates.inc, and emits gates and measurements in circuit order. It formats angles as decimal literals that round-trip to their original Float64 values. See the official gate syntax and measurement syntax. The simulator uses the same half-angle convention and preserves complex phase. OpenQASM standard gates

The simulator evolves a complex128 statevector once per circuit. Logical qubit ID i corresponds to bit i of a basis index. Because all measurements are terminal, sampling the final basis distribution and selecting measured qubits yields the same joint distribution as terminal projective measurements. The printed string starts with measurement bit c[0], corresponding to the first argument of measure. Sampling is deterministic for a fixed circuit, shot count, and seed. The simulator supports up to 16 qubits.

docs.title: Compilation limits
docs.text:
Set qasmith.Compiler.Limits in Go or use the corresponding CLI flags. A zero field or flag selects the default. Limits apply across the reachable compilation and produce a source-aware diagnostic when exceeded.

Limit Default CLI flag Total loop iterations 10,000 --max-loop-iterations Generated gates 100,000 --max-gates Allocated qubits 4,096 --max-qubits Compile-time array slots 32,768 --max-array-elements Static evaluation depth 256 --max-depth Static evaluation steps 1,000,000 --max-steps

Nested expansions share the loop budget. Array slots count across array construction and host boundary copies, including the outer slots of a matrix. Static evaluation steps count evaluated expressions, statements, calls, and blocks. A failed compilation produces no partial circuit. The local simulator keeps its independent 16-qubit limit.

docs.title: Terminal circuit producers
docs.text:
Semantic analysis tracks ordinary quantum effects through function calls. A trusted terminal producer returns a typed recipe for a complete circuit. Lowering validates fresh IR and records the source origin. Prepared circuits may be exported or sampled, and supported variational recipes may be optimized separately. See the execution plan lifecycle.

Generic Smith model transformations retain immutable QUBO snapshots and charge construction work before allocation. Conversion to Ising occurs when the QAOA plan is created. See model immutability.

docs.title: Circuit construction
docs.text:
Use a quantum register to allocate several qubits at once. A compile-time loop can apply a gate to each element. This program is available as examples/register.smith.

fn main() -> MeasuredResult {
    let q = qreg(4);
    for i in 0..len(q) {
        h(q[i]);
    }
    return measure(q);
}

go build ./cmd/qasmith
./qasmith check examples/register.smith
./qasmith compile examples/register.smith
./qasmith run examples/register.smith --shots 4096 --seed 17

The circuit has four logical qubits and four measurements. In the ideal simulator, each of the 16 bitstrings has probability 1/16. The result string starts with the measurement of q[0].

docs.title: Borrow registers in reusable functions
docs.text:
A function can borrow a register of a declared size. It can also accept an array of angles. This is the helper in examples/quantum/layers.smith.

pub fn applyLayer(q: QReg<4>, angles: Float[4]) -> Void {
    for i in 0..4 {
        rz(angles[i], q[i]);
    }
}

The layer example imports this helper and a separate preparation function. The compiler checks both signatures, binds the original logical qubits, and evaluates the angles from the caller's array.

docs.title: Build circuits from a matrix
docs.text:
examples/circuit_builder.smith uses an immutable matrix of Float angles and the imported Smith implementation of RZZ. It visits pairs in increasing index order. The condition selects just the six pairs with i < j.

for i in 0..len(q) {
    for j in 0..len(q) {
        if i < j {
            rzz(weights[i][j], q[i], q[j]);
        }
    }
}

The complete example starts with four H gates and lowers each RZZ to CX, RZ, CX. With the default pass configuration, the backend receives 22 gates and four terminal measurements. Loop indices, matrix access, and branch selection are resolved during compilation.

./qasmith compile examples/circuit_builder.smith
./qasmith run examples/circuit_builder.smith --shots 4096 --seed 17

Use q[i] directly in a call such as cx(q[i], q[j]). The reference keeps the caller's qubit identity. A separate binding such as let a = q[0]; is rejected. To select measurement order, use explicit arguments such as return measure(q[3], q[1]);.

docs.title: Design Philosophy
docs.text:
The core library is intentionally minimal and focused on:

  • Essential primitives: Common quantum gates and operations
  • No external dependencies: Always available, versioned with compiler
  • Predictable behavior: Pure quantum operations without side effects
  • Clear naming: Descriptive names that match quantum computing conventions

For more specialized functionality, create reusable packages and distribute them via the module system.

docs.title: Extending the Qasmith Compiler in Go
docs.text: Use .smith packages to distribute functions written in Qasmith. Use the Go API when an embedding application needs to register a trusted intrinsic, run an IR pass, or select a backend. Go extensions are compiled into the embedding program and registered by that program. The standalone CLI exposes built-in operations.

docs.title: Register a host intrinsic
docs.text:
The following Go function can be part of a custom host. It exposes flipTwice with a single borrowed qubit argument.

import (
    "github.com/quvly/Qasmith/pkg/extension"
    "github.com/quvly/Qasmith/pkg/ir"
    "github.com/quvly/Qasmith/pkg/qasmith"
)

func compilerWithGates() (qasmith.Compiler, error) {
    registry := &extension.Registry{}
    err := registry.Register(extension.Intrinsic{
        Namespace: "example",
        Name:      "flipTwice",
        Signature: extension.Signature{
            Parameters: []extension.Type{extension.Qubit},
            Return:     extension.Void,
        },
        Lower: func(ctx extension.LoweringContext, args []extension.Value) (extension.Value, error) {
            for range 2 {
                if err := ctx.ApplyGate(ir.X, args[0].Qubit); err != nil {
                    return extension.Value{}, err
                }
            }
            return extension.Value{Type: extension.Void}, nil
        },
    })
    return qasmith.Compiler{Registry: registry}, err
}

Source programs explicitly import the registered name:

import { flipTwice } from "host:example";

fn main() -> MeasuredResult {
    let q = qubit();
    flipTwice(q);
    return measure(q);
}

A signature can use classical and Qubit parameters and return a classical type or Void. A classical intrinsic must be pure and has no qubit parameters. Declare distinct qubit operand pairs in Signature.Distinct for static alias checking through helper calls. An optional Validate callback checks concrete argument values during lowering. Check validates signatures and distinct operands without running either callback.

Call ApplyGate synchronously during lowering. It accepts supported typed gates and borrowed qubits from that call. The host API has no allocation, measurement, or raw QASM emission operation. Callback code has ordinary Go privileges and is part of the trusted executable. Source modules and manifest files cannot load native extensions.

docs.title: Replace the backend or add passes
docs.text:
Implement ir.Backend with Name and Compile, then assign it to qasmith.Compiler.Backend. A nil backend selects OpenQASM.

Implement ir.Pass with Name and Run, then add it to qasmith.Compiler.Passes. Passes run in slice order and their output is validated. For example, set Passes: []ir.Pass{qasmith.CancelAdjacentX{}} to cancel consecutive X gates on the same qubit. Omit passes to retain the original instruction stream. Use Compiler.Lower to inspect the typed circuit directly.

docs.title: Parameterized gates
docs.text:
For rotations, assert ctx to extension.ParameterizedLoweringContext and call ApplyParameterizedGate(ir.RZ, []float64{angle}, q). It checks gate arity, finite angles, and borrowed qubits. Existing callbacks still receive extension.LoweringContext and can keep calling ApplyGate for fixed gates.

Use keyed Go literals for extension.Value and ir.ApplyGate. These structs gained the Float and Parameters fields respectively. Fixed gates omit Parameters.

For example, migrate an old positional value literal to extension.Value{Type: extension.Int, Integer: 42} and an old positional gate literal to ir.ApplyGate{Gate: ir.X, Qubits: []ir.QubitID{q}, Origin: origin}. The original Register signature, callback signature, and fixed-gate interface still work with these literals.

docs.title: Boolean and array values
docs.text:
Use extension.Bool and the Value.Bool field for Boolean signatures and values. Build fixed-size classical array types with extension.ArrayType. For example, extension.ArrayType(extension.ArrayType(extension.Int, 2), 3) represents Smith's Int[2][3]. Use Value.Array with an extension.ArrayValue containing the typed elements. The compiler validates returned shapes, element types, and finite floats. It copies arrays at the callback boundary to protect source-level immutability.

Host gate callbacks can still borrow individual qubits, including q[i] from Smith. Registers and arrays of qubits are unavailable in host signatures. For existing host names that became Smith keywords, import the original registration name under an alias, such as import { if as test } from "host:example";.

Phase 2B adds fields to extension.Value and qasmith.Compiler. Use keyed Go literals for both structs. The host registration and lowering callback signatures are unchanged.

docs.title: Trusted modules and opaque values
docs.text:
Register named structured types and explicitly exported compile-time functions through the existing registry. A terminal producer returns a typed circuit plan through a separate controlled callback. Existing borrowed-gate intrinsics remain supported. See the host optimization extension guide.

The QUBO standard library uses the existing trusted registry. Numeric array signatures can constrain either the rank alone or the rank and numeric leaf type.

docs.title: Language reference
docs.text:
A source module contains import and fn declarations. Prefix an exported function with pub. Parameters and return types are explicit. Functions use lexical scopes with immutable parameters and let bindings. Statements end with a semicolon. Comments start with // or are enclosed by /* and */.

fn add(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int {
    let result = a + b;
    return result;
}

fn main() -> Int {
    return add(3, 5);
}

Int is a signed 64-bit integer. Float is an IEEE 754 binary64 value. Write 3 for an Int and 3.0, 0.5, 1.0e-3, or 2e2 for a Float. The immutable pi constant is available in every module and uses Go's math.Pi.

Unary minus binds before *, /, and %, which bind before + and -. Binary operators of equal precedence associate left to right. Parentheses override precedence. Two integer operands produce an integer result, while mixed arithmetic converts the integer operand to Float. Passing or returning an Int where a Float is expected also widens it. Large integers may lose precision during this conversion. Implicit conversion from Float to Int is an error.

Integer division truncates toward zero. The % operator requires integer operands and its result has the sign of the dividend or is zero. Evaluation rejects division or remainder by zero, integer overflow, and non-finite floats. Numeric functions may call other pure numeric functions, including functions imported from another module.

fn prepare(a: Qubit, b: Qubit) -> Void {
    h(a);
    cx(a, b);
}

fn main() -> MeasuredResult {
    let first = qubit();
    let second = qubit();
    prepare(first, second);
    return measure(first, second);
}

Qubit is an owned resource allocated by let name = qubit(); in a quantum entry point. A helper borrows caller qubits through its parameters. It can apply x, h, cx, rx, ry, and rz or call other helpers. The entry point can allocate individual qubits or registers. The compiler checks that the control and target of every cx refer to distinct qubits, including when the operands are passed through other functions. Local bindings cannot copy qubit references.

Rotation gates accept an angle in radians followed by a borrowed qubit. The compiler evaluates the angle while lowering. Angles can use local values, arithmetic, pi, and calls to pure functions.

pub fn rotate(theta: Float, q: Qubit) -> Void {
    ry(theta / 2.0, q);
}

The example rotation module exports rzz(theta, a, b). It applies cx(a, b), rz(theta, b), and cx(a, b). The two qubit operands must be distinct, including when the function is called through imported wrappers.

MeasuredResult is the return type for a quantum entry point. Its final statement is return measure(q, ...); with one or more distinct qubit arguments. Argument order determines measurement bit order. The entry point can allocate qubits that do not appear in the returned measurement. Helpers cannot allocate or measure qubits.

Void functions can end implicitly or with a bare return;. Only Void calls can be used as statements. An entry file must declare a parameterless main returning Int or MeasuredResult. Direct and indirect recursion are rejected.

docs.title: Registers and fixed-size arrays
docs.text:
qreg(size) allocates a register in a let binding in the quantum entry point. The size is a positive compile-time Int and may be computed by a pure function. QReg<N> in a function signature borrows exactly N qubits from the caller. The caller owns the register. Register bindings and individual qubit references cannot be copied into another let binding.

q[i] is a reference to the original qubit. Use it directly as a gate, helper, or measurement argument. Indexes are zero-based compile-time integers. measure(q) measures the whole register in increasing index order. To specify individual qubits or change the order, pass distinct qubit arguments. A single measurement expression accepts either one register or individual qubits.

Classical arrays are immutable values with a fixed shape and a single element type. Nested arrays must be rectangular. An empty array literal has no inferable type. Each array element has the same type, so use [1.0, 2.0] for Float[2]. Index nested arrays from the outside in. The rightmost dimension is outermost. For example, Int[2][3] is three rows of two integers, so values[1][0] selects the second row's first element. Arrays can be passed, returned, and bound to another local name. len() returns the outer length of an array or the size of a register.

docs.title: Compile-time control
docs.text:
Bool values are true and false. Use == and != on two Boolean or two numeric operands. Ordering comparisons <, <=, >, and >= accept numeric operands. Mixed numeric comparisons use the same Int-to-Float widening as arithmetic.

From tightest to loosest, precedence is indexing, unary - and !, multiplication and division operators, addition and subtraction, ordering comparisons, equality comparisons, &&, and ||. The Boolean operators short-circuit. Both operands still undergo type checking.

A for i in start..end loop uses increasing integers from start inclusive to end exclusive. Both bounds must be compile-time Int values. Equal bounds give zero iterations. The loop binding is immutable and local to the loop body. Loops can nest and can use outer loop bindings.

An if condition must be a compile-time Bool. An optional else supplies the other branch. Both branches are type-checked. Only the selected branch is evaluated and emits circuit operations. Aliasing checks on indexed qubits use their actual logical IDs after selection and expansion. Measurement remains a terminal return at the top level of the quantum entry function.

See the circuit construction guide for complete examples.

docs.title: Opaque optimization values
docs.text:
The compiler-distributed optimization modules expose OptimizationProblem, an immutable typed compile-time value. A local Smith function can return it or accept it as a parameter. A terminal circuit-producing call is allowed only as the final return from the quantum entry point, with no separate quantum effects. See the language integration guide.

Use the QUBO standard library to build immutable optimization objectives in pure Smith.

docs.title: Creating a New Project
docs.text:
Use the qasmith init command to create a new project:

qasmith init my-project

This creates: - qasmith.toml - Project manifest - src/main.smith - Entry point with a Bell state example - README.md - Project documentation - .gitignore - Git ignore rules

You can specify a template:

qasmith init my-project --template bell
qasmith init my-project --template ghz
qasmith init my-project --template superposition

docs.title: Entry Point
docs.text:
The entry point is the .smith file that contains the main() function. By convention, this is src/main.smith, but you can specify a different entry point when running commands:

qasmith run src/main.smith
qasmith compile src/main.smith -o output.qasm

docs.title: Module Resolution
docs.text: Qasmith's module resolution system determines how import statements are resolved to actual files. The resolver follows a specific order and enforces security constraints.

docs.title: Resolution Order
docs.text:
When resolving an import, Qasmith checks the following locations in order:

  1. Standard Library (std/ prefix)
  2. Built into the compiler
  3. Always available

  4. Version matches compiler version

  5. Declared Dependencies (package imports)

  6. Look up package name in qasmith.toml or qasmith.json dependencies
  7. Resolve to package root directory

  8. Resolve module path within package

  9. Relative Imports (./ or ../ prefix)

  10. Resolve relative to importing file's directory
  11. Validate within project or package root
  12. Prevent path traversal attacks

docs.title: Resolution Algorithm
docs.text:
For import "std/module":
  1. Check if module is registered in standard library
  2. Return trusted module reference
  3. Fail if not found

For import "package/module":
  1. If package == "std", use standard library
  2. Else look up package in manifest dependencies
  3. Resolve module path within package root
  4. Validate path is within package root
  5. Load and cache module

For import "./path" or "../path":
  1. Resolve relative to importer's directory
  2. Determine package root (project or dependency)
  3. Validate resolved path is within package root
  4. Load and cache module

docs.title: Security Constraints
docs.text:
The module resolver enforces several security constraints:

  • Path Traversal Prevention: Imports cannot escape their package root
  • Symlink Validation: Symlinks are resolved and validated
  • No Absolute Paths: Imports cannot use absolute paths
  • Circular Dependency Detection: Circular imports are detected and reported
  • Case-Insensitive Collision Detection: Prevents issues on case-insensitive filesystems

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: Modules are cached by their canonical path to prevent: - Duplicate loading of the same file - Infinite loops from circular imports - Inconsistent module identity

docs.title: Import Syntax
docs.text: Qasmith supports three types of imports:

docs.title: Relative Imports
docs.text:
Import modules relative to the current file's location:

// Import from the same directory
import { function1 } from "./module.smith";

// Import from a parent directory
import { function2 } from "../libraries/utils.smith";

// Import from a subdirectory
import { function3 } from "./algorithms/grover.smith";

docs.title: Package Imports
docs.text:
Import from declared dependencies:

// Import from a package
import { feature } from "package-name/module";

// Import with alias
import { long_name as short } from "package/utils";

docs.title: Standard Library Imports
docs.text:
Import from the Qasmith standard library:

// Import optimization modules
import { qaoa } from "std/optimization/qaoa";
import { tsp } from "std/optimization/tsp";
import { qubo } from "std/optimization/qubo";

docs.title: Import Specifiers
docs.text:
You can import multiple symbols and use aliases:

import {
    function1,
    function2 as func2,
    function3
} from "./module.smith";

docs.title: Project Manifest
docs.text: The project manifest defines project metadata and dependencies. Qasmith supports both TOML and JSON formats, with TOML being preferred.

docs.title: TOML Format (Preferred)
docs.text:
Create a qasmith.toml file:

name = "my-quantum-project"
version = "0.1.0"

[dependencies]
quantum-utils = { path = "../shared/quantum-utils" }
my-library = { path = "./libs/my-library" }

docs.title: JSON Format (Alternative)
docs.text:
Create a qasmith.json file:

{
  "name": "my-quantum-project",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "dependencies": {
    "quantum-utils": { "path": "../shared/quantum-utils" },
    "my-library": { "path": "./libs/my-library" }
  }
}

docs.title: Required Fields
docs.text:
• name: Project name (must match pattern ^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_-]*$)
  • version: Semantic version (e.g., "0.1.0", "1.2.3")

docs.title: Optional Fields
docs.text: • dependencies: Map of package dependencies

docs.title: Dependency Declaration
docs.text:
Dependencies are declared with a name and a local path:

[dependencies]
package-name = { path = "./path/to/package" }

Constraints: - Package names must match pattern ^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_-]*$ - Package names are case-insensitive - The name "std" is reserved for the standard library - Dependencies cannot overlap with the project root - Dependencies cannot overlap with each other - Paths can be relative or absolute

docs.title: Dependency Structure
docs.text:
A dependency package should have its own manifest:

my-library/
├── qasmith.toml
├── module1.smith
└── module2.smith

The dependency's manifest is not required for path-based dependencies, but recommended for clarity.

docs.title: Standard Library
docs.text: The Qasmith standard library provides trusted modules for common quantum operations.

docs.title: Optimization
docs.text:
import { qaoa } from "std/optimization/qaoa";
import { tsp } from "std/optimization/tsp";
import { qubo } from "std/optimization/qubo";

QAOA (Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm): - Solves combinatorial optimization problems - Accepts optimization problem definitions - Returns quantum circuits for QAOA

TSP (Traveling Salesman Problem): - Encodes TSP instances as optimization problems - Converts distance matrices to QUBO formulations

QUBO (Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization): - Tools for building QUBO models - Constraint handling - Objective function construction

docs.title: Using Standard Library
docs.text:
import { qaoa } from "std/optimization/qaoa";
import { tsp } from "std/optimization/tsp";

fn main() -> MeasuredResult {
    let distances = [
        [0, 10, 15, 20],
        [10, 0, 35, 25],
        [15, 35, 0, 30],
        [20, 25, 30, 0]
    ];

    let problem = tsp(distances, 0);
    return qaoa(problem, [0.4], [0.3]);
}

docs.title: Project Organization
docs.text:
1. Use src/ for source code: Keep your main source files in src/ for clarity
  2. Organize by feature: Group related modules in subdirectories
  3. Use descriptive names: Choose clear, descriptive names for modules and functions
  4. Document public APIs: Use comments to document public functions

docs.title: Import Guidelines
docs.text:
1. Prefer package imports over relative imports: Use package imports for better clarity
  2. Keep import paths short: Avoid deeply nested module structures
  3. Use aliases for clarity: When importing multiple functions, use aliases to avoid name collisions
  4. Group imports logically: Organize imports by standard library, packages, and relative imports

docs.title: Dependency Management
docs.text:
1. Use semantic versioning: Follow semver for your project versions
  2. Pin dependency paths: Use relative paths for reproducible builds
  3. Test dependency updates: Always test after updating dependencies
  4. Document dependencies: List dependencies in your README

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
1. Review dependencies: Only use dependencies from trusted sources
  2. Validate paths: Ensure dependency paths are within expected directories
  3. Avoid absolute paths: Use relative paths for portability
  4. Test on multiple platforms: Ensure paths work on Windows, macOS, and Linux

docs.title: From JSON to TOML
docs.text:
If you have an existing qasmith.json manifest, you can migrate to TOML:

Before (qasmith.json): 

{
  "name": "my-project",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "dependencies": {
    "my-lib": { "path": "./libs/my-lib" }
  }
}

After (qasmith.toml): 

name = "my-project"
version = "0.1.0"

[dependencies.my-lib]
path = "./libs/my-lib"

Both formats are supported, so migration is optional.

docs.title: From Flat Structure to Organized Structure
docs.text:
If you have a flat project structure:

project/
├── main.smith
├── utils.smith
└── algorithms.smith

You can reorganize to:

project/
├── qasmith.toml
├── src/
│   ├── main.smith
│   ├── utils.smith
│   └── algorithms.smith
└── README.md

Update your imports accordingly:

// Before
import { helper } from "./utils.smith";

// After (if you move main.smith to src/)
import { helper } from "./utils.smith";  // Still works with relative imports

docs.title: "undeclared package"
docs.text:
Cause: You're trying to import from a package that's not declared in your manifest.

Solution: Add the package to your qasmith.toml:

[dependencies.my-package]
path = "./path/to/package"

docs.title: "path escapes root"
docs.text:
Cause: An import is trying to access a file outside the project or package root.

Solution: Ensure your import paths don't use ../ to escape the project root. Restructure your project if needed.

docs.title: "circular module dependency"
docs.text:
Cause: Two or more modules import each other, creating a cycle.

Solution: Refactor to break the cycle. Extract shared code into a separate module.

docs.title: "expected a regular .smith file"
docs.text:
Cause: The resolved path doesn't point to a .smith file.

Solution: Ensure your import path ends in .smith for relative imports.

docs.title: Debugging Imports
docs.text:
Use the qasmith deps command to see the resolved dependency tree:

qasmith deps src/main.smith

This shows all modules that will be loaded, helping you identify resolution issues.

docs.title: Example 1: Simple Project
docs.text:
hello-quantum/
├── qasmith.toml
└── src/
    └── main.smith

qasmith.toml: 

name = "hello-quantum"
version = "0.1.0"

src/main.smith: 

fn main() -> MeasuredResult {
    let q = qubit();
    h(q);
    return measure(q);
}

docs.title: Example 2: Project with Libraries
docs.text:
quantum-project/
├── qasmith.toml
├── src/
│   ├── main.smith
│   └── algorithms/
│       └── grover.smith
└── libraries/
    └── utils.smith

qasmith.toml: 

name = "quantum-project"
version = "0.1.0"

src/main.smith: 

import { grover_search } from "./algorithms/grover.smith";
import { helper } from "../libraries/utils.smith";

fn main() -> MeasuredResult {
    let q = qreg(3);
    grover_search(q);
    return measure(q);
}

src/algorithms/grover.smith: 

pub fn grover_search(q: QReg<3>) -> Void {
    // Grover's algorithm implementation
}

libraries/utils.smith: 

pub fn helper() -> Int {
    return 42;
}

docs.title: Example 3: Project with Dependencies
docs.text:
my-app/
├── qasmith.toml
└── src/
    └── main.smith

quantum-utils/  (separate repository)
├── qasmith.toml
├── rotations.smith
└── measurements.smith

my-app/qasmith.toml: 

name = "my-app"
version = "0.1.0"

[dependencies.quantum-utils]
path = "../quantum-utils"

my-app/src/main.smith: 

import { rzz } from "quantum-utils/rotations";
import { measure_all } from "quantum-utils/measurements";

fn main() -> MeasuredResult {
    let q = qreg(2);
    rzz(0.5, q[0], q[1]);
    return measure_all(q);
}

docs.title: Modules and imports
docs.text:
Each .smith file defines a module with its own scope. Import a symbol using its exported name, and optionally bind it under a local alias.

import { prepareBell as entangle, flip } from "./quantum/gates.smith";
import { add } from "./math.smith";
import { rzz } from "core/rotations";

docs.title: Import Types
docs.text: Qasmith supports three types of imports:

docs.title: Core Library
docs.text:
Import from the embedded standard library:

import { rzz } from "core/rotations";
import { bell } from "core/gates";
import { abs, max } from "core/math";

The core library is bundled with the compiler and always available. See Core Library for the full API reference.

docs.title: Relative Imports
docs.text: Relative imports include the .smith extension and start at the importing file's directory. The compiler resolves symbolic links and checks that a relative import stays inside its project or package root. It loads a shared module once per compilation and reports import cycles with the chain of files.

docs.title: Package Imports
docs.text:
Import from declared dependencies:

import { prepareBell } from "entangle/bell";

A bare package/module import uses a dependency name from the entry project's manifest. Packages can import their own files using relative imports, or refer to another dependency by a name declared in that same manifest.

docs.title: Visibility and Scope
docs.text:
Export a function by writing pub fn. A function defined with fn is private. An exported function can call private helpers or imported symbols in its defining module. Callers only see functions they import by name. Local declarations and bindings may not reuse an imported name.

Calls resolve lexical bindings first, then module functions, explicit imports, and compiler built-ins. A lexical value used as a callee is an error. The original gate, allocation, and measurement built-in names are reserved for module declarations and import aliases. len and qreg resolve as built-ins when there is no earlier binding, so existing functions with those names remain callable. The new control-flow and Boolean keywords are reserved in Smith source. The pi constant is also reserved in local bindings and parameters. A module's imports are never implicitly re-exported.

docs.title: CLI Commands
docs.text:
Use qasmith check program.smith to validate every function in the resolved graph, and qasmith deps program.smith to print source-file dependencies. Shared modules are marked after their first occurrence.

Imported functions can accept fixed-size arrays and borrowed registers using the same signature checks as local functions. See register helpers and layers.

Trusted standard modules are resolved from explicit registrations and support import aliases and use from local packages. See the standard optimization modules.

docs.title: Creating Your First Qasmith Package
docs.text:
1. Create packages/entangle/bell.smith and export a reusable function.
fn internalPreparation(q: Qubit) -> Void {
    h(q);
}

pub fn prepareBell(a: Qubit, b: Qubit) -> Void {
    internalPreparation(a);
    cx(a, b);
}
  1. Declare the local directory in qasmith.toml at the project root.
name = "qasmith-example"
version = "0.1.0"

[dependencies.entangle]
path = "./packages/entangle"
  1. Import the exported function in program.smith.
import { prepareBell } from "entangle/bell";

fn main() -> MeasuredResult {
    let a = qubit();
    let b = qubit();
    prepareBell(a, b);
    return measure(a, b);
}
  1. Compile and run. The generated circuit applies a Hadamard to the first qubit and a controlled X to the pair. Simulation produces 00 and 11.
qasmith deps program.smith
qasmith compile program.smith
qasmith run program.smith --shots 1000 --seed 17

docs.title: Project Manifests
docs.text: The compiler looks for the nearest qasmith.toml (preferred) or qasmith.json above the canonical entry file. Without a manifest, the entry file's directory is the project root.

docs.title: TOML Format (Recommended)
docs.text:
name = "my-quantum-project"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A quantum computing project"

[dependencies]
quantum-utils = { path = "../shared/quantum-utils" }

docs.title: JSON Format
docs.text:
{
  "name": "my-quantum-project",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "dependencies": {
    "quantum-utils": { "path": "../shared/quantum-utils" }
  }
}

Dependency names start with an ASCII letter and may contain ASCII letters, digits, hyphens, and underscores. Dependency paths are relative to the manifest unless absolute and must point to real directories. Roots must be distinct and non-overlapping with other dependency roots. Packages may be inside the project or declared outside it.

The std/ and core/ namespaces are reserved. Compilation uses local files and does not fetch packages or run installation scripts.

docs.title: Limitations and proposed milestones
docs.text:
Phase 2B provides fixed-size quantum registers and classical arrays, compile-time loops and conditions, static rotation angles, and terminal measurement. Quantum helpers borrow existing resources. The ideal local simulator supports up to 16 qubits. Compilation can produce larger circuits within its independent resource limits.

Arrays are immutable and their dimensions are fixed. Registers have concrete sizes in signatures. Source programs cannot use runtime parameter binding, measurement feedback, runtime control flow, mutation, recursion, closures, or generic types. Native runtime plugins, remote dependencies, and hardware-specific transpilation remain outside the current compiler.

Phase 2C adds standalone QUBO and Ising mathematics with a bounded classical reference solver. Phase 2D adds generic QAOA generation, expectation evaluation, and bounded hybrid parameter search through Go and the QUBO JSON CLI. Phase 3A adds the fixed-start TSP application through Go and CLI. Phase 3B adds trusted Smith optimization modules, opaque compile-time values, and execution plans. Smith optimization guide

  • Extend the standard library with compiler-distributed Smith code using the existing trusted module boundary.
  • Establish ancilla ownership and uncomputation rules before introducing reversible integer arithmetic.
  • Explore symbolic circuit parameters and additional targets while preserving typed IR.
  • Add package metadata and dependency version selection before introducing a remote package registry.

Phase 3C adds user-defined QUBOs, generic penalties, and immutable composition through reusable Smith packages. Phase 4A adds the VS Code extension and standalone LSP. See the editor tooling guide.

docs.title: Phase 4B recommendations
docs.text:
• Improve recovery across multiple independent parse and semantic errors in a single file.
  • Add incremental synchronization and dependency-aware indexing before extending references beyond loaded module graphs.
  • Add document links for import paths and evaluate safe quick fixes for compiler diagnostics.
  • Establish platform-specific CLI distribution and VSIX release verification before publishing the extension.

docs.title: CLI Overview
docs.text: The Qasmith CLI provides commands to check, compile, run, and optimize Qasmith programs. This guide covers every command and common options.

docs.title: Global options
docs.text:
All commands accept:

  • -h, --help — show help for a command
  • Exit status is 0 on success, 1 for compilation or execution errors, and 2 for invalid CLI usage.

docs.title: qasmith version
docs.text:
Print the installed version:

qasmith version

docs.title: qasmith check <file>
docs.text:
Check a program for errors without producing output:

qasmith check bell.smith

docs.title: qasmith deps <file>
docs.text:
List module dependencies:

qasmith deps bell.smith

docs.title: qasmith compile <file>
docs.text:
Compile a .smith file to OpenQASM 3.0:

qasmith compile bell.smith
qasmith compile bell.smith -o output.qasm

By default, output is written beside the source file with a .qasm extension.

docs.title: qasmith run <file>
docs.text:
Compile and run a program with the built-in statevector simulator:

qasmith run bell.smith --shots 1000 --seed 17

Options:

  • --shots N — number of measurement shots (default: 1000)
  • --seed N — random seed for reproducibility (default: varies)

docs.title: qasmith eval <file>
docs.text:
Evaluate a classical program:

qasmith eval examples/classical.smith

docs.title: qasmith optimize <file>
docs.text:
Compile and run a QAOA optimization problem:

qasmith optimize program.smith --max-evals 200 --restarts 3 --shots 1000 --seed 42

Options:

  • --max-evals N — maximum function evaluations
  • --restarts N — number of optimizer restarts
  • --shots N — measurement shots per evaluation
  • --seed N — random seed
  • -o <file> — write optimized OpenQASM output

docs.title: qasmith qaoa optimize <problem>
docs.text:
Run QAOA optimization on a JSON problem file:

qasmith qaoa optimize problem.json --layers 1 --max-evals 200 --restarts 3 --seed 42 -o optimized.qasm

docs.title: First Program
docs.text: This guide walks you through writing, compiling, and running your first Qasmith program. You'll create a Bell state circuit and measure the result.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Qasmith CLI installed — see Installation

docs.title: Create a Bell state
docs.text:
Save the following code in a file called bell.smith:

fn main() -> MeasuredResult {
    let a = qubit();
    let b = qubit();
    h(a);
    cx(a, b);
    return measure(a, b);
}

This program:

  1. Allocates two qubits a and b
  2. Applies a Hadamard gate to a, putting it in superposition
  3. Applies a CNOT gate with a as control and b as target, entangling them
  4. Measures both qubits and returns the result

docs.title: Check the program
docs.text:
Verify the program is well-formed:

qasmith check bell.smith

check reports any errors but does not emit output. Exit status is 0 on success, 1 for errors.

docs.title: List dependencies
docs.text:
See the modules this program depends on:

qasmith deps bell.smith

docs.title: Compile to OpenQASM 3.0
docs.text:
Compile the program to OpenQASM 3.0:

qasmith compile bell.smith

This writes bell.qasm next to the source file. Specify a different output path with -o:

qasmith compile bell.smith -o output.qasm

The generated OpenQASM looks like:

OPENQASM 3.0;
include "stdgates.inc";

qubit[2] q;
bit[2] c;

h q[0];
cx q[0], q[1];
c[0] = measure q[0];
c[1] = measure q[1];

docs.title: Run the simulation
docs.text:
Run the program with the built-in statevector simulator:

qasmith run bell.smith --shots 1000 --seed 17

You should see roughly equal counts for 00 and 11, confirming the Bell state:

00: 498
11: 502

docs.title: Run a classical program
docs.text:
Qasmith can also run classical programs that compute with integers and floats. Save this as classical.smith:

fn main() -> Int {
    let x = 3 + 5;
    return x;
}

Run it with:

qasmith eval classical.smith

Output:

8

docs.text: Qasmith is available for macOS, Linux, and Windows. Both installers verify the executable's SHA-256 checksum. Releases support x86-64 and ARM64 on all three platforms.

docs.text:
curl -fLO https://github.com/quvly/Qasmith/releases/latest/download/install.sh
sh install.sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
qasmith version

The installer defaults to ~/.local/bin. Add the export line to your shell configuration (~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, etc.) to keep the binary on your PATH across sessions.

Use --version v0.9.1 to pin a release or --bin-dir DIRECTORY to choose a destination.

git clone https://github.com/quvly/Qasmith.git

fn main() -> MeasuredResult {

    return measure(q);
}

This program: 1. Creates a 2-qubit register 2. Applies a Hadamard gate to the first qubit (creating superposition) 3. Applies a CNOT gate (creating entanglement) 4. Measures all qubits

This creates a Bell state, where the qubits are entangled and will always measure the same value.

docs.title: Quantum Optimization in Qasmith
docs.text: Qasmith includes built-in support for quantum optimization through QUBO models, Ising formulations, and the QAOA algorithm. This section guides you through building and solving optimization problems with quantum circuits.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Quantum optimization maps a problem onto an energy function and finds the lowest-energy state using a quantum circuit. Qasmith supports the full workflow:

  1. Model — express your problem as a QUBO or Ising model
  2. Compile — generate a QAOA circuit from the model
  3. Optimize — tune circuit parameters to minimize energy
  4. Decode — interpret the measurement result as a solution

docs.title: QUBO (Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization)
docs.text:
Express a problem as a quadratic function of binary variables:

$$\min_{x \in {0,1}^n} x^T Q x$$

  • QUBO Language Guide — use QUBO in Smith code
  • QUBO Go API — use QUBO from Go
  • Custom Models — build your own QUBO models

docs.title: Ising Model
docs.text:
Map a problem to spin variables:

$$\min_{s \in {-1,+1}^n} \sum_i h_i s_i + \sum_{i<j} J_{ij} s_i s_j$$

  • Ising Model Guide — formulation and conversion

docs.title: QAOA (Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm)
docs.text:
Run a variational quantum circuit to approximate the optimal solution:

  • QAOA Guide — full QAOA workflow
  • QAOA Circuits — circuit structure
  • QAOA Evaluation — measure and interpret results

docs.title: Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP)
docs.text:
A complete application solving the TSP with quantum optimization:

  • TSP Guide — API, limits, and route interpretation

docs.title: Standalone libraries
docs.text:
The Go packages under pkg/optimization build and evaluate QUBO and Ising models, convert between energy conventions, add penalties, serialize models, and solve small QUBOs by bounded exhaustive search.

go run ./examples/optimization/qubo

See the QUBO guide and optimization architecture.

docs.title: Smith-language integration
docs.text:
Build optimization models directly in Smith code:

import "std/qubo" as qubo;

fn main() -> MeasuredResult {
    let model = qubo::new(2);
    qubo::linear(model, 0, -1.0);
    qubo::linear(model, 1, -1.0);
    qubo::quadratic(model, 0, 1, 2.0);
    return qubo::solve(model);
}
